title: usage-signal-orthogonalization-cheatsheet
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact working cheat-sheet for turning a large, noisy set of adoption/usage signals into a compact, near-orthogonal scoring vector for customer health. Goal is to reduce redundant signals, avoid double-counting, and make weights interpretable for playbooks and escalation routing.

Context / Motivation:
- CS team currently has ~45 candidate metrics across Product, Billing, and Support. Many are highly correlated (e.g., daily-active-api-keys and token-volume).
- Correlated signals inflate sensitivity and create brittle score changes when one upstream metric spikes.
- We want a pragmatic process (not just black-box PCA) that ops/CS can explain to PMs/AE.

High-level approach (3 steps):
1) Signal collection + normalization
   - Collect raw signals for rolling 30/90/180-day windows. Prefer both short-term and long-term windows for the same metric (e.g., 7d and 90d).
   - Normalize to z-scores per cohort (or min-max if required for thresholds). Always keep original unit column for debugging.
   - Example columns: api_calls_7d_z, api_calls_90d_z, token_volume_7d_z, embeddings_count_30d_z, routes_created_90d_z, errors_rate_14d_z, support_tickets_30d_z.

2) Correlation analysis + grouping (practical orthogonalization)
   - Compute pairwise Pearson or Spearman correlation matrix (Spearman if many outliers).
   - Cluster signals into groups with threshold r > 0.6 (adjustable). Use hierarchical clustering (ward) to visualize dendrogram—this gives human-readable groups.
   - For each cluster pick: representative feature OR combine via weighted mean (internal variance used as inverse weight).
   - Quick rule: if two signals have r > 0.85, collapse into single canonical signal (e.g., api_calls_7d + token_volume_7d => request_intensity_7d).

3) Orthogonalization / de-correlation pass (optional but recommended)
   - Two pragmatic options:
     A) Gram-Schmidt-style orthogonalization on the representative feature set (keeps interpretability but creates non-intuitive transformed features).
     B) PCA on cluster-averaged features and label top components with human-readable names ("Engagement-intensity", "Support-friction"). Keep only first N components explaining ~75-85% variance.
   - We prefer option A for playbooks because resulting axes map back to specific signals. Use A when you need direct action routing. Use B for compact dashboards where interpretability can be added as annotations.

Weighting & scoring assembly:
- Start with 4 orthogonal axes: Engagement, Feature-Depth, Latency/Error-Friction, Commercial-Antecedents (billing/contract signals).
- Example final formula (illustrative):
  health_score_raw = 0.40 * Engagement_z + 0.25 * FeatureDepth_z - 0.20 * ErrorFriction_z + 0.15 * Commercial_z
- Transform to 0-100: health_pct = 50 + 10 * health_score_raw (tweak scale to fit desired distribution) OR use sigmoid mapping for smoothing.
- Provide bucket thresholds (initial):
  - Green: health_pct >= 65
  - Yellow: 45 <= health_pct < 65
  - Red: health_pct < 45
- Calibration notes: calibrate using last 12 months of accounts that renewed vs churned, and match histogram percentiles so each bucket has useful population.

Sanity checks / unit tests to add:
- Check month-over-month bucket churn rates align with known cohorts.
- Backtest: holdout last renewal season; compute AUC of health_pct predicting renewal. Aim AUC > 0.72 initially.
- Explainability test: for 20 random accounts that flip bucket, provide top-3 contributing signals in natural language.

Operational playbook mapping (example):
- If account enters Red and has ErrorFriction_z > 1.2 -> Trigger SRE + CSM high-touch (alert template #err-friction-1).
- If account enters Yellow and Engagement drops by >= 1 sigma (relative week-over-week) -> AE outreach + product adoption workshop.
- If Commercial_z indicates overdue invoice but technical signals are Green -> AE-led billing touch + extend trial credit (no SRE).

Example sample calculation (toy):
- Inputs (z-normalized representatives): Engagement=0.8, FeatureDepth=0.2, ErrorFriction=1.1, Commercial=-0.3
- health_score_raw = 0.40*0.8 + 0.25*0.2 - 0.20*1.1 + 0.15*(-0.3) = 0.32 + 0.05 - 0.22 - 0.045 = 0.105
- health_pct = 50 + 10*0.105 = 51.05 -> Yellow bucket (close to Green)
- Top contributors: Engagement (+0.32), ErrorFriction (-0.22), FeatureDepth (+0.05)

Practical tips & gotchas:
- Avoid mixing raw counts with rates in the same axis unless carefully normalized (counts scale with ARR/cohort size).
- Keep cohorting around ARR or seat count for normalization; smaller accounts will otherwise be noisy.
- Don’t overfit to AEs — keep at least 2 independent signals per axis so individual metric manipulations don’t spoof a healthy score.
- Maintain a "debug view" that includes original raw signals, z-scores, cluster membership, and the intermediate axis values. This is crucial for QBR storytelling.

Implementation checklist (immediate next steps):
- [ ] Export last 18 months of candidate signals (CS-CSIG-EXPORT JIRA).
- [ ] Run correlation matrix and produce cluster dendrogram (owner: DataOps, ticket JIRA-CS-789).
- [ ] Propose canonical representative features for each cluster (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Implement Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization function in cs-signal-tooling repo (PR #56).
- [ ] Backtest on 6/12/18 mo windows and produce AUC table by cohort.

Questions for review:
- Thresholds: r > 0.6 clustering vs r > 0.7? Which matches business sensitivity better?
- How many axes should product accept for rollout? (3 vs 4 vs 5)
- Sigmoid vs linear scaling for final score — prefer linear until adoption, then consider smoothing.

Notes-to-self:
- Keep simple initial UX for CSM console: top-3 signals + single traffic-light score.
- Capture case studies for 5 accounts where orthogonalization prevented false positives.

References / links: see linked_artifacts above. Also: internal notebook: /notebooks/signal-orthog-proto.ipynb (DataOps), and PR draft #56 for implementation.

Next meeting: internal CS + Data call Wed 2025-03-05 10:00 PT to lock clustering threshold and pick representative features.
